title: TB8-09389
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): XXXX XXXX XXXX (Appellant) is a citizen of Kenya who is appealing a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD), dated March 19, 2018, rejecting her claim for refugee protection on the basis that she has an Internal Flight Alternative (IFA) in Nairobi or Mombasa.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: I dismiss this appeal. XXXX XXXX XXXX (Appellant) is a citizen of Kenya who is appealing a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD), dated March 19, 2018, rejecting her claim for refugee protection on the basis that she has an Internal Flight Alternative (IFA) in Nairobi or Mombasa. She fears that if she returns to Kenya her husband will subject her to domestic violence and force her and their children to undergo Female Genital Mutilation (FGM). She is asking the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) to substitute the RPD determination for a positive one, or in the alternative, refer this matter back to the RPD for redetermination. She has submitted new evidence and requested an oral hearing. I have accepted some of this new evidence but rejected the request for an oral hearing. Based on my independent review, I find that the Appellant has a viable IFA in Nairobi or Mombasa and this is determinative of her appeal.

After considering the Appellant's arguments and all of the evidence, I dismiss her appeal and confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention1 refugee nor a person in need of protection, pursuant to section 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).2 I find that the Appellant could live safely in Nairobi or Mombasa and that this relocation would not be objectively unreasonable for her.
Only some of the evidence presented by the Appellant is accepted.

I observe at the outset that the new evidence submitted for this appeal was challenging to assess as some of this evidence is not new as it was previously before the RPD, some of the exhibits presented as new evidence had information missing, the source of the information was unclear for some documents and there is minimal argument as to how the evidence presented meets the required criteria. Notwithstanding these issues, the following documentation was sought by the Appellant to be entered as new evidence: 1) A Wikipedia article on female genital mutilation of unknown date; 2) NYT article on FGM dated January 13, 2018; 3) Guardian article on FGM in Kenya dated December 23, 2016; 4) a document called "The challenge of eradicating FGM" of unknown date and unknown source; 5) a series of pages which appear to be related to "FGM/Plan International" of unknown date; 6) a document called "This practice should be stopped" dated January 22, 2018; 7) a document called "Female Genital Mutilation: Kenya's worst-kept secret" dated February 16, 2017 from the Daily Maverick; 8) a document called "Female Genital Mutilation in Kenya" dated September 21, 2015; 9) a document called "FGM among the Maasai community of Kenya dated March 8, 2005 of unclear source; 10) Al Jazeera article titled "Magazine: A Witness to FGM" dated July 10, 2015; 11) Reuters article titled "Kenyan doctor goes to court to legalize female genital mutilation" dated January 19, 2018; 12) a medical report dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 2018; 13) Appellant's CV letter from XXXX XXXX dated XXXX XXXX, 2018; 14) photos of unknown date and unknown persons with the Appellant; 15) photos of unknown date with the Appellant alone or with unknown persons; 16) a medical letter dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 2018; and, 17) the Appellant's Basis of Claim (BOC) form.

According to the law,3 I can only accept evidence that: i. arose after the RPD decision; ii. was not reasonably available at the time of the decision; or iii. that you could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to bring to the RPD before the decision.
If the evidence meets one or more of these requirements, I must decide if the evidence is new, credible and relevant before I can accept it.4

The Appellant's Memorandum outlines the criteria that guide my assessment of new evidence for this appeal5 but the only reason that I can locate regarding how the new evidence meets these criteria is that the Appellant's former Counsel was not experienced and failed to provided sufficient and satisfactory evidence to the RPD. I do not find this explanation adequate or sufficient to address how the Appellant's new evidence meets the strict requirements.

I decline to accept items #1 through #11 as I find that all these documents were reasonably available to the Appellant to present to the RPD. The Appellant's general assertion that her past Counsel was not experienced is inadequate to explain why all of these items, which are all readily and publicly available, could not have been presented to the RPD. There is no evidence before me to indicate that a formal complaint has been launched against the Appellant's past Counsel.

I decline to enter item #12 which is a Canadian medical report relating to the Appellant's left knee ultrasound as I find that this document has no relevance to the determinative issue in this appeal, which is the viability of an IFA in Kenya. Again, I note that there is no submission as to how this document meets the required criteria.

Items #14 and #15, which represent pictures of an unknown date which appear to be the Appellant with unknown persons, I also decline to enter as new evidence as I find that this evidence is not relevant to the determinative issue of IFA. There is also no explanation provided to me as to the significance of these pictures and why these pictures were not provided to the RPD.
The last item, #17 which is the Appellant's BOC form, I decline to enter as this is in the RPD Record and is not new evidence.

The only evidence I will accept for this appeal is item #13 (Appellant's CV letter from XXXX 2018) and item #18 (medical letter relating to an assessment and report conducted in XXXX 2018), as I find that these two documents arose after the RPD decision and have relevancy in my assessment of the reasonableness of an IFA for the Appellant in Kenya. RAD RULE 296

Further evidence was submitted to the RAD subsequent to perfection of the appeal. I also found this application confusing as the same argument regarding the inadequacy of the Appellant's Counsel before the RPD was advanced as the reason why this evidence could not be submitted. Further, the evidence to be entered under RAD Rule 29 was not readily found with the application. Despite these challenges, I believe that the only documents which the Appellant sought to enter under RAD Rule 29 included: 1) a report dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 20187 from Dr. XXXX; and 2) a support letter from a Canadian church dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 20188.

As this evidence was submitted following perfection, I must consider this "new" evidence, pursuant to RAD Rule 29: Documents or written submissions not previously provided - person 29 (1) A person who is the subject of an appeal who does not provide a document or written submissions with the appellant's record, respondent's record or reply record must not use the document or provide the written submissions in the appeal unless allowed to do so by the Division. Application (2) If a person who is the subject of an appeal wants to use a document or provide written submissions that were not previously provided, the person must make an application to the Division in accordance with rule 37. Documents - new evidence (3) The person who is the subject of the appeal must include in an application to use a document that was not previously provided an explanation of how the document meets the requirements of subsection 110(4) of the Act and how that evidence relates to the person, unless the document is being presented in response to evidence presented by the Minister. Factors (4) In deciding whether to allow an application, the Division must consider any relevant factors, including (a) the document's relevance and probative value; (b) any new evidence the document brings to the appeal; and (c) whether the person who is the subject of the appeal, with reasonable effort, could have provided the document or written submissions with the appellant's record, respondent's record or reply record.

In assessing the proposed new evidence in the RAD Rule 29 application, I also note the cases of Semykina9and Arisekola10 which state that unlike section110(4)11 applications, even if a proposed document would otherwise be rejected under the statutory requirements of section110(4), the Singh12 and Raza13 factors must still be considered.

I will enter into evidence the report dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 2018 as I have accepted the Appellant's explanation that there were issues with assessor availability and the time required to complete the report. I find the report to have some relevance to my IFA analysis. I will not enter into evidence the support letter from a Canadian church as there is no explanation provided as to why such a letter could not have been provided to the RPD or with the perfection of this appeal. I also find that the content within this letter is not relevant to the determinative issue in this appeal which is the viability of an IFA for the Appellant in Kenya.

The Appellant has requested an oral hearing. While I did accept some new evidence, I find that this evidence does not raise a credibility issue or concern. Accordingly, I am unable to hold an oral hearing.

My role is to look at all the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.14 In making this assessment, I have considered all the evidence, including the written transcript of the RPD hearing, as well as the Chairperson Guidelines 4: Women Refugee Claimants Fearing Gender-Related Persecution (Gender Guidelines).15 I find that the determinative issue in this appeal relates to the viability of an IFA, so this will be my focus. IFA Test for IFA

The test to apply in order to determine whether a viable IFA exists is two-pronged and requires that the RPD find, on a balance of probabilities, that: (i) there is no serious possibility of the Claimant being persecuted or subjected, on a balance of probabilities, to a danger of torture or to a risk to their life or of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment in the proposed IFA area; and, (ii) conditions in the IFA area must be such that it would not be unreasonable, in all the circumstances, including those particular to the Claimant, for the Claimant to seek refuge there.16 The threshold is very high for the unreasonable test.17 Prong 1: The Appellant would not be at Risk in the IFA

Mombasa and Nairobi were proposed as a possible IFAs at the start of the RPD hearing. The Appellant testified that her husband was motivated to search for her and her daughters everywhere in Kenya and would be capable of tracking her through her mobile phone or the school registration data base.

In considering the forward-facing risk of harm that the Appellant might face in the IFA locations of Mombasa or Nairobi, I have considered whether the agent of persecution (which is the Appellant's husband in this case) is motivated and capable of locating the Appellant in these IFA locations. Insufficient Evidence that the Appellant's Husband is Motivated to Search For Her

When asked by the RPD if her husband was searching for her, she testified that he had been. She stated that her mother told her some new people she did not know were asking about the Appellant, but she did not know who these people were and whether they were members of her husband's family.18 When asked if her adopted daughter (who is of adult age and lives in Kenya) had any contact with her husband, the Appellant stated "No, I don't think so."19 The Appellant was then asked if her Aunt, who provided a letter of support, has had any contact with anyone asking about the Appellant, and her response was she had not asked her Aunt but that she would not tell anybody, even if they asked about her.20 The Appellant similarly said her mom would also not reveal her whereabouts. No further evidence was adduced by the Appellant that any of her numerous siblings, who are still in Kenya, had any contact from her husband or had contact with persons asking about her whereabouts. Based on this evidence, the RPD found that it was more likely than not that the husband had made no efforts to locate her. My assessment of the evidence finds the same and I note that on appeal there is no rebuttal of this finding.

In my consideration of the motive of the Appellant's husband to persecute her, I note that it is nearing four years since the Appellant's arrival in Canada and there is no credible evidence that her husband has sought her whereabouts or the whereabouts of their two daughters who have remained in Kenya during this time. Further, the Appellant's two supporting affidavits, which are both dated in XXXX 2016, note no contact from the Appellant's husband or his family for purposes of seeking the Appellant or her children.21 Means and Ability of the Appellant's Husband to Find Her in the IFAs is Not Established

The Appellant testified that her husband could easily find her in the IFA locations because when you buy a SIM card for your mobile phone, there is a number provided which makes it easy to trace a person's whereabouts and asserted that there is no way to protect the privacy of your mobile phone number and location in Kenya. The RPD observed that the Appellant had provided no evidence or any explanation as to how her husband would get her cellphone number if she did not give him the number, and that her explanation that there was no privacy in Kenya did not mean that there would be a way for her husband to find her cellphone number if she chose not to give it to him.

On appeal it is argued that in this day of the internet and cellphone that it is not impossible to track someone through their personal phone number. Other than this general assertion, no further argument or evidence is provided as to how the Appellant's husband would be able to accomplish this. It is further submitted that the Appellant testified that her husband's family had come to her mother in order to find out about the Appellant and her daughters. The Appellant further states that it seems to be a grave travesty of justice that the RPD stated that the Appellant's husband would not be able to get her cellphone if she did not give him the number.

First, I find that the Appellant's testimony did not indicate that her husband's family had visited her mother in Kenya looking for the Appellant and the daughters. The transcript of the RPD hearing clearly indicates that the Appellant's mother told her that some new people she did not know were asking about the Appellant, but that her mother did not know who these people were and whether they were members of her husband's family.22

Regarding the submission on appeal that it would not be impossible to track someone through their personal phone number, I observe that I have no further evidence before me as to how the Appellant's husband would be able to do so. Even if I were to accept that there may be some way for the Appellant to be located, for example through her old mobile phone number or SIM card, I find that the Appellant is not bound to use that phone or that particular SIM card in the future. The RPD observed that the Appellant provided no evidence or explanation regarding how her husband would be able to get her cellphone if she did not give him the number herself. I do not agree with the Appellant that this statement by the RPD is a travesty of justice.

Aside from speculation that her husband could find her through her mobile phone, the Appellant did not provide credible objective evidence to establish mobile phone interception or surveillance that could place her at risk of harm. There is no evidence before me that any of the Appellant's family members, who remain in Kenya, have been contacted by her husband or members of her husband's family through their cell phones or any other means. I also observe that there is no evidence that the Appellant has received any unwanted contact from her husband on her cell phone or by other means since her arrival in Canada more than three and a half years ago. Therefore, on a balance of probabilities, I find that her husband would not be able to locate her through telecommunications, and a mobile phone specifically, if she were to return to Kenya.

The second way the Appellant believed her husband could track her down in the IFA locations related to what she stated was one school registry in Kenya and her belief that the Ministry of Education in Kenya would readily provide her husband with details of their whereabouts. She testified that the Ministry would hand out information about all the children registered in schools to anybody who was asking and anybody can go with a bribe and be provide with the information.23 The RPD found that there was no objective information which indicated how information about students was stored, whether information such as addresses were recorded, or its accessibility by members of the public. Accordingly, the RPD found that the Appellant's beliefs about being found through the school registry was speculative and not supported by any objective evidence. The RPD further noted that the Appellant's testimony regarding school registry documentation was in contrast to her earlier testimony that she did not need any documents, such as a birth certificate, to register her children in school. I observe on appeal that these findings are not rebutted, and I see no error here.

I have also considered the Appellant's risk related to her being forced to undergo FGM. I considered the country documentary evidence which indicates that FGM is illegal in Kenya, but the practice continues with around 21% of women having undergone the procedure. It is performed mostly on girls between the ages of 12 and 18, but sometimes as young as seven. Prevalence is reported to vary across ethnic groups, but is highest amongst the Somali, Samburu, Kisii, and Maasai communities. Women/girls living in towns and cities are generally less likely to be subject to FGM than those living in rural areas.24 Further, objective documentation also indicates that the Kenyan government has made efforts to end FGM with various anti-FGM programs being run in partnership with international agencies and has successfully prosecuted a number of FGM practitioners. In addition, various Non-Governmental Organisations provide support and assist girls who wish to avoid undergoing FGM in obtaining protection. In general, the country documentation indicates state protection is likely to be available. And, if a woman/girl who is at real risk of FGM, or their accompanying family, is at risk of serious harm for opposing the procedure in their home area, they may be able to relocate to another area where they would not be at risk.25 I also considered evidence that the Kenyan government has made efforts to end the practice, including running various anti-FGM programs in partnership with international agencies. There have also been a number of successful prosecutions of persons performing FGM since 2011, when the FGM law was introduced, and Kenya's anti-FGM prosecution unit has deployed teams across the country in an attempt to prosecute more cases.26

Finally, I considered documentation which indicates that there are differences in the prevalence of FGM between rural and urban areas, with on average 31% of women in the rural areas reporting that they were circumcised, compared to just 17% in urban areas. Education is also a significant factor, with 54% of women without any formal education being circumcised, as opposed to 19% of women who attended secondary school.27 Overall, I find that the country evidence indicates that the Appellant is not the profile of the group of women who have an elevated risk of being subjected to this practice, namely young, uneducated and residing in a rural environment. Thus, based on my assessment of the country documentation evidence, there is not sufficient evidence to demonstrate that the Appellant faces a serious possibility of persecution in the form of forced FGM by her husband in the IFAs.

The National Documentation Package (NDP), item 1.7 suggests that the constitution and laws of Kenya provide for freedom of movement, and the government generally respects this in practice.28 The documentation indicates that there are several very large, multilingual, multiethnic cities in Kenya, such as Mombasa (1.1 million) and Nairobi (3.9 million) where persons fleeing non-state actors may be able to safely relocate and establish themselves based on their own particular circumstances.29 The documentation also notes that there are significant numbers of women living alone in Nairobi and it is very possible for single women to be employed in the city depending on their level of education.30

I note that gender-based persecution including domestic violence and FGM continue to be problems in Kenya, but find that the Appellant has not established that she faces a serious possibility of such persecution in the proposed IFAs on this basis.

Having considered all of the evidence, I find that the Appellant has not discharged her burden to show that she would face a serious possibility of persecution or would be subjected to a personal risk to life, risk of torture or risk of cruel and unusual punishment or treatment, on a balance of probabilities, in Nairobi or Mombasa. Proposed IFA areas are reasonable

The RPD considered the Claimant's personal circumstances and found that Nairobi and Mombasa were reasonable places to relocate to and that the Appellant would not face undue hardship in relocating there. In reaching this determination, the panel was guided by the Federal Court of Appeal's decision in Ranganathan, which set a very high threshold for what makes an IFA unreasonable.31 The courts have repeatedly outlined that the threshold requires, at a minimum, the proof of adverse conditions which would jeopardize the life or safety of the claimant in relocating, demonstrated based on actual and concrete evidence.

The RPD observed that the Appellant did not identify any particular hardship associated with relocating within Kenya, and her concerns about re-location stemmed from her belief that her husband would be able to locate her. In its analysis of the reasonableness of the IFA locations, the RPD considered the psychological evidence which includes a diagnosis of XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX as well as XXXX XXXX XXXX secondary to the separation from her daughters. The RPD found that the Appellant could continue with the management of her mental health in Kenya and that being re-united with her daughters may improve the symptoms related to her depression. In addition, the RPD considered the documentary evidence which indicated that there were a large number of single and divorced women living in Nairobi who have escaped gender-based violence and that many women choose to live alone. The RPD also considered the Appellant's unique circumstances which mitigated against the IFA locations being unreasonable. Specifically, the Appellant testified that she had previously resided in Nairobi where she was gainfully employed. She was also able to successfully establish a business in a new Kenyan community with no family resources where she was able to support her family with little assistance from her husband. Based on all of the above, the RPD found that it would not be unduly difficult for the Appellant to similarly establish herself in one of the IFA locations.
There are no specific arguments presented on appeal as to how or why the RPD erred in finding that the IFA locations of Nairobi or Mombasa were reasonable.

In my assessment of the reasonableness of the IFA for the Appellant, I have also taken into consideration the new evidence which relates to the Appellant's physical injuries and current mental health issues. There is a report from Dr. XXXX XXXX,32 dated XXXX XXXX, 2018, which represents a one-hour assessment with the Appellant. Dr. XXXX indicates she has read the Appellant's BOC form, but she does not outline what other documentation, if any, was accessed to corroborate the self-reported information. The report observes that the Appellant had a prior psychological assessment conducted on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2016, but Dr. XXXX does not indicate if she had access to this earlier assessment. I also note that Dr. XXXX indicates that her report is focused on incidents that caused personal injury, but that she would comment on the Appellant's mental health. A letter from Dr. XXXX, also dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 2018 explains that due to time constraints she was unable to complete an updated XXXX assessment. Dr. XXXX report describes in some detail a number of specific incidents of domestic violence which the Appellant disclosed as being caused by her husband, and there are pictures of the Appellant's physical injuries. In the summary section of the report, Dr. XXXX opines that the Appellant bears physical signs and ongoing symptoms consistent with her experience of gender based violent including physical and verbal abuse in Kenya at the hands of her husband for refusing to undergo or let the children undergo FGM. Turning to the Appellant's mental health, Dr. XXXX notes that the Appellant's anxiety, depression and insomnia improved when she found work as a personal support worker with people with disabilities but that there has been a re-emergence of mental health symptoms due to her refugee claim being denied. It is reported that the Appellant has reduced her hours at work. It is recommended by Dr. XXXX that the Appellant would benefit from receiving on-going counselling and support and that her family doctor follow up with her for continued management of her mental health symptoms. Dr. XXXX makes no specific recommendation related to the reasonableness of the Appellant returning to Kenya.

I find that I can put little weight on the recent report from Dr. XXXX in relation to my analysis of the reasonableness of the IFA for the Appellant. The report itself represents a one-hour session which is primarily focused on a review and analysis of the Appellant's past physical injuries. This information is of minimal relevance to my assessment of the reasonableness of the IFA locations of Nairobi and Mombasa. Further, this report which is based on a one hour interview does not represent a comprehensive psychological assessment of the Appellant's mental health circumstances, and the measures or assessment instruments used to evaluate the Appellant's mental health are not detailed.

I find that the Appellant's current mental health issues do not render the IFA locations unreasonable. There is country information that in Kenya, services such as mental health are available and accessible in the cities of Nairobi and Mombasa. Further, big government hospitals offer services to victims of gender based violence; they have "Gender Based Violence Recovery centres."33 The Appellant has not provided any evidence to establish that she would be unable to access mental health services in Kenya.

Finally, I have also considered the new evidence which indicates that the Appellant has improved her education in Canada by completing a diploma program as a XXXX XXXX XXXX.34 She has secured employment in this area in Canada. The Appellant was able to complete this education successfully while also managing her mental health issues. These factors mitigate against the IFAs in Kenya being unreasonable, as the Appellant will be returning with an improved educational and work profile which will assist her in finding employment. Further, as noted by the RPD, the Appellant was gainfully employed in Kenya in another field.

I note that the "burden does not fall on the RAD to explain why the proposed IFA would be safe" for the Appellant.35 The onus is on the Appellant to demonstrate why the proposed IFA is not reasonable. The Appellant has not adduced evidence that demonstrates it is not objectively unreasonable or unduly harsh for her to seek refuge by relocating to and residing in Nairobi or Mombasa. I agree with the RPD that Nairobi or Mombasa are reasonable IFAs. In order for an IFA to be considered unreasonable, conditions in the proposed IFA would have to jeopardize the life or safety of the Appellant, and this is not the finding of the RAD.

In addition, I find that the consideration of an IFA is determinative under sections 96 and 97 of the IRPA.36 I have found that the Appellant has a viable IFA in her home country and as such, the Appellant is not a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection.

This independent analysis of the evidence reveals that the RPD did not err on the availability of an IFA, and its decision is correct. The RPD conducted a clear and well-reasoned IFA analysis, and correctly concluded that an IFA exists given the facts and evidence of this case. The Appellant has failed to establish a serious possibility of persecution, or that she could be personally subjected to a risk to life or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or to a danger of torture, if she relocated to Nairobi or Mombasa. Moreover, the Appellant did not establish that it would be objectively unreasonable or unduly harsh for her to relocate to Nairobi or Mombasa. This finding is determinative of the appeal.

I dismiss the Appeal and confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection, pursuant to section 111(1)(a) of the IRPA.37 (signed) Kim Polowek Kim Polowek September 30, 2020 Date 1 1951 Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees: Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, "Handbook on Procedures and Criteria for Determining Refugee Status", under the 1951 Convention. 2 Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), S.C. 2001, c. 27. 3 IRPA, section 110(4). 4 Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v.
